newsitem.title: JAPAN: INTERVIEW-JAFCO not worried by fierce competition.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-JAFCO not worried by fierce competition.

text.p: Japan Associated Finance Co Ltd (JAFCO), the nation's largest venture capital firm, played down fears that rising competition was cutting profits and making it harder to find promising ventures to invest in.
JAFCO, a unit of Nomura Securities Co Ltd, also said that its business will not be affected by its parent company's illegal stock transactions for a corporate racketeer.

"It is true that there has been a shortage in the number of promising venture firms, but there are still a number of firms that we can invest in," Mitsumasa Murase, president of JAFCO, told Reuters in a recent interview.

Asked if JAFCO plans to increase investment in relatively new venture firms, Murase said: "It is not very realistic to place too much weight on investment in newborn firms, as in Japan it takes many years, a little less than 30 years on average, for venture firms to go public."
He said JAFCO's investment will centre on venture firms that have been in business for some years.

"Our investment in firms that have just started business is only slightly above 10 percent, in terms of the number of firms we invest in, and only a few percent in terms of our total amount of investment. I don't think the ratios will change greatly in the near future," he said.
Competition in the industry is intensifying due to the growing number of venture capital firms affiliated with banks.
Their strategy of providing help to ventures just before they go public differs from JAFCO's, however, which provides firms with funds at an earlier stage, Murase said.

He added that JAFCO's risk management is superior to other venture capital firms because its investments are spread out among a large number of firms, totalling 1,700, of which more than 430 have gone public.
Murase also said JAFCO would aim to increase its earnings per share at a pace two to three times Japan's nominal economic growth.
Regarding the Nomura scandal, he said: "There might be some damage to our image, but there has been no damage at all to our business."
He said he was worried, however, that companies that Nomura lead manages might delay plans to go public.
Murase also said that the price of JAFCO's shares, which are traded over-the-counter (OTC), seems to be at an appropriate level considering the sluggish condition of Japan's OTC market.
He added, however, that he felt OTC stock prices in general were undervalued.

"If OTC market prices were to correct, I think it would not be surprising to see our company's share price rebounding to levels around 11,000 to 12,000 yen, which some analysts say is an appropriate price," he said.
In late Friday trade, JAFCO shares stood at 6,950 yen, unchanged from Thursday's close.
